content: The document titled Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene (WASH) in Health Care Facilities: Practical Steps to Achieve Universal Access to Quality Care outlines the critical importance of ensuring access to clean water, proper sanitation, and hygiene services in health care settings. It emphasizes that health care facilities lacking these basic necessities pose significant risks to patient safety, dignity, and public health. Such deficiencies can exacerbate the spread of infections, including antimicrobial-resistant pathogens, and undermine efforts to improve maternal and child health outcomes. The publication highlights that globally, WASH services in health care facilities are substandard, with many facilities lacking access to safe water, sanitation, and hand hygiene infrastructure. For example, over 5 billion people rely on health care facilities without adequate sanitation services, and many more lack access to proper hand hygiene and waste management systems. These challenges are more pronounced in rural areas and low-income countries, where health care facilities are three times more likely to lack water services compared to those in higher-income settings. The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) emphasize universal health coverage, including access to WASH services, as a prerequisite for quality care. WASH is particularly vital for safe childbirth and infection prevention. The document underscores that inadequate WASH services contribute to maternal and neonatal deaths, with infections accounting for 26% of neonatal deaths and 11% of maternal mortality globally. In lowand middle-income countries, health care-associated infections (HCAIs) are twice as prevalent as in high-income countries, with 15% of patients developing infections during hospital stays. The document outlines eight practical steps to improve and sustain WASH services in health care facilities. These include conducting situation analyses, setting national targets, improving infrastructure, establishing accountability mechanisms, monitoring progress, engaging communities, training health workers, and conducting operational research. It also stresses the importance of integrating WASH into national health policies, budgets, and quality improvement plans. The publication further highlights the association between hand hygiene and infection prevention, citing historical and contemporary evidence. For instance, Dr. Ignaz Semmelweis demonstrated in the 19th century that strict hand hygiene protocols significantly reduced maternal mortality rates. Modern studies confirm that improved hand hygiene practices reduce the incidence of HCAIs. Additionally, the document addresses the role of WASH in combating antimicrobial resistance (AMR). Inadequate WASH services in health care facilities contribute to the spread of resistant infections and increase the reliance on prophylactic antibiotic use, further driving AMR. Unsafe disposal of health care waste, including wastewater, can also spread resistant pathogens into the environment and communities. The publication identifies barriers to implementing WASH in health care facilities, such as incomplete standards, lack of funding, and insufficient integration into broader health programs. It calls for coherent national standards, adequate funding, and cross-sectoral collaboration to address these challenges. The document concludes by emphasizing the solvability of the WASH crisis in health care facilities and the significant return on investment in improving these services.
